lesson.title: The Power to Say What the Law Is
lesson.summary: In 1803 the Supreme Court claimed the authority to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution, a power with no explicit textual basis that has shaped American government ever since.
lesson.body:
Judicial review is the power of federal courts, and ultimately the Supreme Court, to strike down a law or executive action that conflicts with the Constitution. Nothing in the Constitution's text explicitly grants this power, which is one reason it took a sharp political crisis to establish it. That crisis arrived in 1803 with the case of Marbury v. Madison, decided by Chief Justice John Marshall, and it remains the foundation of American constitutional law.

The case grew out of the bitter transfer of power from the Federalist John Adams to the Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson after the election of 1800. In his final days in office, Adams and the outgoing Federalist Congress created new judgeships and rushed to fill them, a group later nicknamed the midnight judges. William Marbury was appointed a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia, but his commission was not delivered before Adams left office. The new secretary of state, James Madison, acting under Jefferson's direction, refused to hand it over. Marbury sued, asking the Supreme Court to issue a writ of mandamus ordering Madison to deliver the commission, relying on a provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that let the Court hear such cases directly.

Marshall faced a trap either way. If the Court ordered Madison to act, Jefferson's administration might simply ignore it, exposing the Court's weakness. If the Court backed down, it would look powerless from the start. Marshall found a third path. He ruled that Marbury did have a right to his commission and that withholding it was illegal, but that the Supreme Court itself had no authority to issue the writ in this particular case. The reason was that the Judiciary Act of 1789 had expanded the Court's original jurisdiction beyond what Article III of the Constitution allowed, and Congress could not enlarge the Court's constitutional powers through an ordinary statute. Because the law conflicted with the Constitution, Marshall declared that section of it void.

That last move was the real point of the decision. By striking down part of an act of Congress, the Court asserted for itself the authority to judge when laws violate the Constitution, a role Alexander Hamilton had defended years earlier in Federalist No. 78 but which no court had yet actually exercised. Marshall reasoned that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, that courts are bound to apply the Constitution over conflicting statutes, and that it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.

The decision was clever politically as well as legally. Jefferson could hardly object loudly, since the ruling denied Marbury the job he wanted, yet it planted a much larger precedent. Judicial review gave the Supreme Court a lasting check on Congress and the presidency, a power the Court would use again decades later in cases such as Dred Scott v. Sandford and, eventually, Brown v. Board of Education. It also completed a triangle of institutional power, alongside the elected presidency and Congress, that continues to shape how laws are made, challenged, and overturned in the United States today.
